section.title: A Picture That Takes Work
section.para: Some pictures take a lot of computing. This one asks every point of the picture how soon it runs away when a little sum is repeated on it — the Mandelbrot set. The work is one for over the points, and the rounds of that loop do not depend on each other.

So nothing in the program says how it runs, and below the program you can choose: on one core of your computer, on all of them, or on the graphics card. The picture is the same; the time is not. relaxed lets the card compute a little less strictly.
section.programlisting:
function colour(x: i32, y: i32, w: i32, h: i32) returns u32 { let cr (x as f32) * 3.0 / (w as f32) - 2.1 let ci (y as f32) * 2.0 / (h as f32) - 1.0 var zr: f32 0.0 var zi: f32 0.0 var k: i32 0 while k < 200 and zr * zr + zi * zi <= 4.0 { let t zr * zr - zi * zi + cr zi := zr * 2.0 * zi + ci zr := t k := k + 1 } if k = 200 return 0xFF000000 let shade ((k % 32) * 8) as u32 0xFF000000 | ((255 - shade) << 16) | ((shade / 2) << 8) | shade }
let w: i32 600 let h: i32 400 var picture Vector[u32]((w * h) as size_t) relaxed for p in w * h picture.put(p as size_t, colour(p % w, p / w, w, h)) File.write_bytes("mandelbrot.`w`x`h`.rgba", picture.as_bytes()) print "`w * h` points"
section.para: The colour of a point is a number with four bytes — red, green, blue and how opaque it is — and the picture goes into a file whose name says its size; the playground shows such a file. The fractal showcase lets you zoom into it and fifteen more fractals, and race the cores against the card.

When the card took part, its bar shows where the time went: the first run compiles the card's kernel, once; then the data goes to the card and back, the card computes, and its results are read and checked. What is left is the processor's own part of the program.

section.title: Twice the Cores, Half the Time?
section.para: How much faster does a loop get with more cores? “Race” runs the program on one core, on two, on four and so on up to all of them, then on the graphics card, and draws how many times faster each was than one core.

If every core helped fully, the points would lie on the dashed line: twice the cores, half the time. They lie below it. Starting the cores costs a little, the cores share the memory, and many processors have fast cores and economical ones — once the fast ones are all at work, each further core adds less. The card is a line of its own: you do not choose how many of its cores it uses.
section.programlisting:
function colour(x: i32, y: i32, w: i32, h: i32) returns u32 { let cr (x as f32) * 3.0 / (w as f32) - 2.1 let ci (y as f32) * 2.0 / (h as f32) - 1.0 var zr: f32 0.0 var zi: f32 0.0 var k: i32 0 while k < 500 and zr * zr + zi * zi <= 4.0 { let t zr * zr - zi * zi + cr zi := zr * 2.0 * zi + ci zr := t k := k + 1 } if k = 500 return 0xFF000000 let shade ((k % 32) * 8) as u32 0xFF000000 | ((255 - shade) << 16) | ((shade / 2) << 8) | shade }
let w: i32 900 let h: i32 600 var picture Vector[u32]((w * h) as size_t) relaxed for p in w * h picture.put(p as size_t, colour(p % w, p / w, w, h)) File.write_bytes("mandelbrot.`w`x`h`.rgba", picture.as_bytes()) print "`w * h` points"
section.para: Make the picture smaller — 300 × 200 — and race again: with less work, starting the cores weighs more, and the curve flattens sooner.

section.title: When the Card Pays
section.para: The card does not start for nothing: the data goes to it, the card is told to begin, and the results come back — a cost for every loop it runs, however small. This program runs the same loop for more and more points, from 1024 up to a million, and prints how long each took; a Stopwatch measures.

“Compare” runs it three times: on all cores, on the card, and where it pays — there the program decides at every run of the loop where it goes. Below a certain size the cores win, above it the card; the chart marks where.
section.programlisting:
; a little work for each point: a hundred steps of the logistic map function work(i: i32) returns f32 { var x ((i % 1000) as f32) / 1000.0 var k: i32 0 while k < 100 { x := x * 3.9 * (1.0 - x) k := k + 1 } x }
let most: i32 1048576 var out Vector[f32](most as size_t) ; once, small and not timed: the card compiles its kernel here let small: i32 1000 relaxed for i in small out.put(i as size_t, work(i)) var n: i32 1024 while n <= most { let watch Stopwatch.start() relaxed for i in n out.put(i as size_t, work(i)) print "size `n` `watch.milliseconds()`" n := n * 4 }
section.para: The work for a point is a hundred steps of a little formula. Make it a thousand — while k < 1000 — and compare again: with more work in every point, the card pays sooner.

section.title: A Sum, and What f32 Costs
section.para: Not every loop paints a picture. This one estimates the largest singular value of a matrix by multiplying a vector with it again and again — spectral-norm, a classic among benchmarks. Each product is a loop over the rows, and each row a sum over the columns.

The card computes in f32, numbers with about seven digits; the processor has f64 too, with about sixteen. The program does the same work in both, round by round, and draws how many digits of each estimate are right. The f64 loop stays on the processor — a card in the browser has no f64 —, the f32 loop may go to the card.
